newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe defends EU, brands his opponents eccentric.
newsitem.headline: Juppe defends EU, brands his opponents eccentric.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, defending the planned single European currency on Tuesday, branded his election opponents an "eccentric coalition" ranging from Communists to the anti-immigrant far right.

Juppe, under fire from some of his own allies for lacklustre campaigning for the May 25-June 1 general election, urged voters to re-elect his centre-right coalition to give President Jacques Chirac stable government for the next five years.

"This eccentric coalition stretching from the Communist Party to the (far-right) National Front should make voters pause for thought," he told Europe 1 radio, portraying his coalition as a beacon of reason.

Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said on Monday he would prefer an upset win by the Socialist-led opposition to a victory for Juppe, saying the left was more likely to derail Chirac's drive for a single European currency, the euro.
"Let's not be ungrateful to Europe," said Juppe. "If we have peace in Europe, it is due to European integration...We have to make the euro an instrument both of stability and growth."
He dismissed opposition charges that he was planning a new bout of unpopular austerity to help qualify for the euro from 1999 if the centre-right wins.

Both the Communists and the National Front were bitter opponents of the Maastricht Treaty on European union, approved by a wafer-thin majority in a 1992 referendum. The Socialists favour the euro, on certain conditions.

The latest poll, by BVA for Paris Match magazine, projected Juppe's coalition would win between 275 and 331 National Assembly seats to 223-273 for the combined left and 0-2 seats for the far-right National Front.

A separate poll for the daily La Croix showed 30 percent of voters identified with the European policies of the Socialists and an equal number with those of the parties in Juppe's coalition. Just 23 percent identified on Europe with parties opposed to Maastricht like the Communists or the National Front.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin campaigned alongside Greens leader Dominique Voynet, who is also representing the Socialists in a constituency in the Jura in eastern France, and called the centre-right a threat for France at the millennium.

"To have the right, for nine years -- four already, and five more -- to pass the year 2000, I think that it's a major risk for the country," he said. The centre-right won a landslide in 1993 when voters dumped the Socialists.

Jospin, who travelled with Voynet on a barge along a canal to highlight environmental issues, reiterated that the Socialists were willing to lead a broad-based left-wing government including ecologists or Communists.

Juppe charged that Socialist campaign promises were vague and that Jospin still had to explain how he would fund the creation of 700,000 promised youth jobs as part of a drive to cut record unemployment of 12.8 percent.
Juppe, shown by opinion polls to be deeply unpopular, deflected questions about whether he would be staying on as premier if the centre-right won.

"This election is not about choosing a prime minister," Juppe said. "A majority is being chosen." Some politicians in the centre-right coalition have started jockeying for positions should Chirac choose not to reappoint him.

A poll last week showed just nine percent of voters wanted Juppe to stay on as premier, well behind right-wing rivals including his predecessor, Edouard Balladur, and National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin.

The prime minister referred to his reputation as an uncaring technocrat when asked in the radio interview whether he was hurt by such attacks. "Everyone says I'm an insensitive computer, so I don't know why you're asking," he said.
